recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what the two end values are, and where the derivative is zero.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Test the conditions on [−1, 1]
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both ends give 0 because −1 and 1 are the two roots of x² − 1. Write the substitution for each end separately.
steps.memory_tip: When the endpoints of the interval are the two roots of the function, f(a) = f(b) = 0 — but the line still has to be written.
lines: f(x) = x² − 1 is a polynomial function, so
(i) f is continuous on the closed interval [−1, 1]
(ii) f is differentiable on the open interval (−1, 1)
∴ f(−1) = f(1) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies on [−1, 1].

recall.must_convey: That f is a polynomial, continuous on [−1, 1] and differentiable on (−1, 1), and that f(−1) = f(1) = 0 because the endpoints are the roots.
accept: the two endpoints are the roots so both end values are zero
f of minus one is zero and f of one is zero
polynomial, so continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open one

steps.why: Both end values are 0 here because −1 and 1 are exactly the roots of x² − 1. Rolle's theorem is often set on an interval whose ends are two roots of the function, and this question is that shape at its simplest.
common_mistakes: Reading (−1)² as −1, which gives f(−1) = −2 and breaks the third condition.
Assuming the two ends must agree because the interval is symmetric, instead of evaluating f at both.

steps.label: Solve f′(c) = 0 inside (−1, 1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. c must be strictly inside — the theorem never allows c = a or c = b. State the inequality −1 < 0 < 1.
steps.memory_tip: Between two roots of a differentiable function the derivative is zero somewhere, and here that point is the lowest point of the parabola.
lines: −1 < 0 < 1, so c = 0 lies in the open interval (−1, 1)

lines.text: ∴ Rolle's theorem is verified, with c = 0 ∈ (−1, 1)

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 2x gives c = 0, and that 0 lies strictly between −1 and 1.

steps.why: Between two roots of a differentiable function the derivative must be zero at least once, and that is exactly what Rolle's theorem states. Here the single point where it happens is c = 0.
common_mistakes: Giving c = ±1, which are the endpoints; c must lie strictly inside the interval.
Writing c = 0 without the inequality −1 < 0 < 1 that places it inside.
